Good morning everyone,  

 

Three bills were signed in the last week: Oklahoma’s comprehensive privacy law (SB 546), Utah’s privacy amendment for motor vehicle manufacturers (HB 357), and South Dakota’s genetic testing privacy law (SB 49). There were also decisions reached in two significant consumer protection lawsuits concerning youth privacy and online safety. As always, you can find our legislation and state enforcement trackers in the FPF Portal.

💬 New Resource on Oklahoma Comprehensive Privacy Law: Oklahoma has become the latest U.S. state to enact a comprehensive consumer privacy law after Governor Stitt signed SB 546 into law on March 20. SB 546 is a Virginia-style law with few deviations from that model, and it will go into effect on January 1, 2027. See FPF’s analysis here.

 

Stuff from the States 

 

Arizona - ASAA Bill PASSED COMMITTEE (HB 2991): This bill passed out of committee with an amendment on March 25. This bill previously passed the House on March 5. While the bill initially would have regulated minors’ use and access of social media and harmful content, the bill now follows an App Store Accountability Act-style framework. App store providers must conduct age verification and obtain parental consent and share information related to age range and parent consent with developers via age signals.

 

California - DROP Updates: Sen. Becker (D) held a press conference with CalPrivacy this week to provide updates on the DROP system and deletion rights. Later in the week, CalPrivacy announced that they will soon make a DROP Sandbox accessible to data brokers, allowing brokers to develop and validate their integration with DROP and see technical documents. Entities with an account as a data broker in DROP will receive notice of sandbox access to the contact email addresses associated with their account. 

 

Georgia - Comprehensive Privacy Bill Gutted and Amended (SB 111): The proposed Georgia Consumer Privacy Protection Act, which passed the Senate last year but was held in the House committee, appears to be dead—the committee favorably reported a substitute that guts and amends the bill, replacing it with a tax credit bill. 

 

Maine - Comprehensive Privacy RE-PASSED HOUSE (LD 1822): Maine’s comprehensive privacy bill, heavily inspired by Maryland’s law, has re-passed the House after being amended during the concurrence process. The bill will be engrossed and return to the Senate for their concurrence vote. One remaining difference between the two versions of the bill is that the Senate version includes an exemption for political organizations. See FPF’s prior analysis of the bill here.

 

Maryland - Privacy Amendment on Immigration Enforcement PASSED HOUSE (HB 711): As amended, this bill would prohibit a controller from knowingly selling personal data to a governmental unit that, within the prior 6 months, has engaged in or supported civil immigration enforcement through the provision of personnel or material resources. Other changes this bill would make include expanding the definition of precise geolocation data to extend to information identifying the location of a mobile device or vehicle (within 1,750’), adding a sensitive data catch-all for inferences used to indicate a category of sensitive data, and narrows the legal compliance exception with respect to civil immigration enforcement. 

 

Michigan Kids Code Passed Committee (SB 758): This bill passed out of committee on March 25. While the bill is now on third reading, no immediate vote is expected since the Senate has now adjourned until April 14.

 

Minnesota - Autonomous Vehicle Bill Introduced (HF 4521): Rep. Sencer-Mura (D) introduced an autonomous vehicle bill on March 23. While most of the bill is outside of the scope of these updates, it does provide that an “on-demand autonomous vehicle network” would be subject to the Minnesota Consumer Data Privacy Act.

 

New Jersey - Children’s Data Protection Bill Introduced (S. 4016): Sen. Vitale (D) introduced this minor-focused social media privacy bill on March 19. This bill would require covered entities reasonably likely to be accessed by children to conduct data protection impact assessments (DPIAs), implement default privacy settings for minors, and restrict certain processing activities involving minor data.

 

Oklahoma - Comprehensive Privacy Law ENACTED (SB 546): At long last, we have the 20th state comprehensive privacy law. Governor Stitt signed SB 546 on March 20, concluding Oklahoma’s multi-year effort to enact a privacy law. This is a standard, Virginia-style law. See FPF’s analysis here.

 

South Dakota - Genetic Privacy Law ENACTED (SB 49): South Dakota is the latest state to enact a direct-to-consumer genetic testing privacy law after Governor Rhoden signed SB 49 on March 23. This law regulates direct-to-consumer genetic testing, including by providing for consumer data rights, consent requirements, and data security obligations. See FPF’s overview here.

 

Utah - UCPA Amendment on Vehicle Privacy ENACTED (HB 357): Governor Cox signed HB 357 on March 19. This bill amends the Utah Consumer Privacy Act, expanding coverage to motor vehicle manufacturers who collect personal data through a vehicle data collection system and imposing requirements for in-vehicle privacy controls. See FPF’s analysis here.

 

Vermont - Data Broker Update PASSED HOUSE (H.211): The House passed H.211 on March 25. This bill would update Vermont’s data broker registration law. Changes include updating the definition of brokered personal information (to align more with the definition of personal data in state comprehensive privacy laws), requiring data brokers to provide consumers with a mechanism to have their brokered personal information deleted, and directing the Vermont Secretary of State to study the feasibility of creating a Delete Act-style accessible deletion mechanism. 

 

Federal Happenings

 

State AGs Advocate for Federal Limits on Data Brokerage: A coalition of seventeen state attorneys general have written to the Senate Committee on Homeland Security and Government Affairs Committee and the House Committee on Oversight and Accountability to express their concerns with AI-driven mass surveillance and government purchase of large datasets. The letter includes a number of legislative recommendations, including: prohibiting the federal government from purchasing sensitive personal data (including data associated with AdIDs or MAIDS) or web browsing data; requiring judicial warrants for law enforcement access to web browsing data, search queries, location information, and “using AI to identify data subjects”; closing “foreign surveillance loopholes” that enable domestic surveillance; requiring federal agencies to delete unlawfully collected data and algorithms trained on such data; and baseline data broker regulations.

 

House Considering Modernizing GLBA: The House Committee on Financial Services held a hearing recently on “Updating America’s Financial Privacy Framework for the 21st Century.” The hearing included a discussion draft of a bill that would update title V of the Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act. Amongst the proposed changes are new data minimization requirements that would require financial institutions to limit their collection, use, retention, or disclosure of nonpublic personal information only “to the extent necessary for . . . legitimate business, legal, or regulatory purposes” that are not prohibited under title V. The bill would also allow consumers to opt-out of the disclosure of their nonpublic personal information even after the initial opportunity to opt-out. 

 

In the Courts

 

Consumer Protection Trial Jury Verdicts Returned in New Mexico and California: In two bellwether cases coming out of New Mexico and California this week, juries found companies liable under consumer protection legal theories for platform design failures and misrepresentations of platform safety risks. First, on March 24, a New Mexico jury found that Meta violated the state’s Unfair Practices Act (“UPA”) for “misleading” platform safety to consumers and “endangering children” through platform design choices. Specifically, the jury found that the defendant had engaged in unfair trade practices and misrepresentation through its failure to restrict distribution of CSAM and obtain parental consent for child data collection and use for minors under 13, for designing its platform in a way that was “addictive” and maximized the time children and teens spent on the platform, and for claiming that the platform was safe for children and teens despite known safety risks. The jury ordered the maximum penalty under the law, resulting in a $375M order for damages. Meta has stated it intends to appeal this decision. Notably, the AG’s lawsuit also included a public nuisance claim that was not considered by the jury and is scheduled for bench trial starting May 4. The AG is seeking additional damages against Meta and injunctive relief that would require the company to make platform changes such as implementing “effective age verification, removing predators from the platform, and protecting minors from encrypted communications that shield bad actors.”

 

The following day, a California jury found that Meta and YouTube negligently designed their platforms, leading to plaintiff’s severe mental distress in a consumer-led lawsuit. Specifically, the jury considered whether the platform design features such as infinite scroll and algorithmic recommendations contributed to the plaintiff’s anxiety and depression, ultimately finding in favor of the plaintiff. The jury ordered $3M in compensatory damages for the plaintiff, and the court assessed an additional $3M in punitive damages against the defendants. Google has stated it plans to appeal the verdict. Further FPF analysis on the implications of these verdicts for companies forthcoming.
